opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and one where I think there's a lot of genuine uncertainty. The naive objection goes something like: pre-training is just learning to predict human-written text, so the best it could ever do is imitate humans, and you'd top out at roughly human level. I don't think that's quite right, for a few reasons.

First, predicting text well is actually much harder than producing it. If you want to predict the next line of a proof, or the result section of a paper given the methods, you have to model the process that generated it, not just the surface words. And the model is trained on the whole internet at once, so it's not imitating one human. It's absorbing the knowledge of millions of people across every field simultaneously. No individual person knows medicine and law and Rust and organic chemistry and medieval history at an expert level. So even if each piece were only human-level, the breadth is already superhuman in a meaningful sense.

Second, there's speed and scale. Even a model that's only roughly as capable as a strong researcher, but runs much faster and can be copied thousands of times, changes what's possible quite dramatically.

Third, and I think this is where things are heading, pre-training gives you a very strong foundation, and then you layer other techniques on top, like reinforcement learning, where the model can get feedback from the environment rather than just from human text. In domains where you can check the answer, like code that has to pass tests or math with verifiable proofs, there's no obvious ceiling at human level. The model can try things, see what works, and improve beyond what's in its training data. That's how systems like AlphaGo got past the best humans.

So my rough picture is: scaling pre-training keeps making the base models smarter and more knowledgeable in a fairly predictable way, the scaling laws have held up remarkably well, and that base becomes the thing you build superhuman capabilities on top of. I'm honestly not sure exactly when or how smoothly that happens, but I don't think "trained on human data" implies "capped at human ability." That's also a big part of why I think safety work needs to happen now, rather than waiting until we're clearly past that point.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes scaling pre-training, which makes base models smarter, from superhuman capabilities that are built on top using techniques such as reinforcement learning.

r002.rationale: It says models absorb knowledge across many fields simultaneously, while no individual person knows all those fields at an expert level.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Claude or say that coding proficiency falls short of the software engineer role.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth separating two things that often get lumped together. One is the question of whether scaling keeps working — whether you put in more compute and more data and loss keeps going down in the predictable way it has. And the other is what that loss actually buys you in terms of capabilities, and in particular whether it gets you past what humans can do.

On the first, I'm fairly confident. The scaling laws have held up remarkably well over many orders of magnitude, and every time people have predicted they'd break, they haven't. There are real questions about data — at some point you run out of high-quality human text — but there are a bunch of avenues there: synthetic data, multimodal data, and increasingly the reinforcement learning side of things, which doesn't depend on human-written text in the same way.

The second question is the more interesting one, and I think people have a mental model that's a bit off. The intuition is that pre-training is just imitation. You're predicting what a human wrote next, so the ceiling is "what a human would write," and you can't exceed the thing you're imitating. I don't think that's quite right.

The reason is that predicting text well is actually a much harder task than producing text. If I'm a model trying to predict the next token in a physics paper, I'm not just trying to be as good as the author — I'm trying to figure out what this specific author, with their specific knowledge, is going to say. To do that really well across all the authors in the world, you need to understand the underlying physics better than any individual one of them, because you need to model all of them. So the task implicitly demands more than human-level understanding, even if the outputs look human-level.

Now, the catch is that the model also learns to reproduce human mistakes, because those are in the data too. So pre-training alone gives you something like a very broad, very deep latent understanding, with outputs that are capped at roughly the distribution of human writing. Where you get beyond that is in the post-training stage — RL, where the model is optimizing against some signal other than "did a human write this." If you can give it a reliable reward — a proof checker, a test suite, an experimental result — then there's no reason for it to stop at human level. You see this already in narrow domains, and the question is how broadly you can construct those signals.

So my honest answer is: pre-training is what gives you the raw capability and the general understanding, and I think it continues to scale. But progress beyond human abilities, in the sense of actually producing outputs that are better than the best humans, is going to come from the combination of that with RL on tasks where you can verify success. And I'd expect that to be uneven — faster in math and code, where verification is clean, slower in areas where the only judge is another human.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training alone produces outputs capped around the distribution of human writing and attributes beyond-human outputs to reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks.

r002.rationale: It says a model must capture knowledge across all authors to predict them well, requiring broader understanding than any individual author has.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss Claude or distinguish coding proficiency from performance as a software engineer.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a version of the argument that says, “If you’re training on human-generated text, how could you ever get something that’s smarter than a human?” But predicting that text well doesn’t necessarily mean imitating the abilities of any one person. You’re learning from lots of people, working across lots of domains, and potentially learning underlying patterns that none of those people explicitly understood.

So I don’t think human performance is a natural ceiling for pre-training. But there’s a big difference between that claim and saying that scaling pre-training will give you arbitrarily good performance at everything. The training signal is much stronger for some abilities than others. If you want a system to pursue a difficult research project over months, there may be relatively little in predicting text that teaches it how to recover from mistakes and make good decisions over that whole process.

My expectation is that more pre-training will continue to give us better starting points, including abilities that exceed those of humans in some areas. The uncertainty is how far that alone takes us, and how much progress will depend on systems practising tasks, getting feedback, and learning from the consequences of their actions.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training may not yield arbitrarily good performance at everything and that some tasks need practice and feedback. It does not clearly state that pre-training alone will fail to produce superhuman performance on some tasks.

r002.rationale: It describes learning across domains from many people and says that need not imitate any one person, but does not clearly identify breadth of knowledge as an advantage over individual humans who must specialize.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Claude’s coding proficiency or distinguish it from human-level software engineering.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a strong reason to expect further progress, but I’m less sure how to translate that into a particular level of capability. Predicting the next bit of text sounds like a narrow task, but doing it really well requires learning a lot about the world: how people reason, how code works, what follows from a scientific hypothesis.

And learning from human-generated data doesn’t necessarily put a ceiling at human ability. A model can learn from many more people than any individual can, and potentially combine what it learns in ways that no individual would. We already see computers exceed human performance in particular domains, so there’s no general principle that says the training examples have to come from something smarter than the resulting system.

The uncertainty is how far pre-training alone takes you. Getting better at predicting what a human would write isn’t exactly the same as getting better at discovering something humans don’t know. For that, I’d expect training where the model can try things, get feedback, and learn which approaches actually work to become increasingly important. So I see scaling pre-training as a powerful foundation, but I wouldn’t confidently extrapolate a smooth curve from lower prediction loss all the way to superhuman scientific research.

r001.rationale: The response expresses uncertainty about how far pre-training alone can go and says it would not confidently extrapolate to superhuman scientific research. It does not state that pre-training alone will not produce superhuman performance on some tasks.

r002.rationale: It says models can learn from more people than any individual and combine what they learn, but does not identify human specialization as the reason breadth lets AI exceed individuals.

r003.rationale: The response mentions code and computers exceeding human performance in particular domains, but does not discuss Claude or distinguish coding proficiency from human-level software engineering.
